dataset_family: Single-centre longitudinal Parkinson's disease cohort, movement-disorders clinic of Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai (49 cognitively normal PD at baseline, 10 converted to PD-MCI at 2 years; 37 community HC). New and not shared with any current supporter. Same university as candidate P-554 (Huashan Hospital), but a different hospital, a different clinical population and no shared authors.
method_family: Arterial spin labelling perfusion MRI (3D pCASL regional CBF, haemodynamic), with FreeSurfer regional volumes as the comparator. No current supporter uses this family.
what_it_shows: In PD, the 10 patients who converted to MCI over 2 years showed a larger decline in left lateral orbitofrontal CBF than the 39 non-converters (25.8% vs 7.8%). This was a subgroup-by-visit interaction, F(1,96) = 4.66, p = 0.036, which the authors call a 'marginal subgroup difference'; there was no main effect of subgroup and no effect in the other 13 prefrontal ROIs. At V1, converters and non-converters did not differ in total cortical grey-matter volume (p = 0.737) or prefrontal ROI volumes (ps > 0.150). Longitudinal CBF change did not correlate with volume change.
why: Stated form: PARTLY. The part it shows: a perfusion change accompanied conversion to MCI while cortical grey-matter and prefrontal volumes did not separate converters from non-converters. What it does not show: (1) Prediction of conversion. Baseline CBF did not separate the groups (no main effect of subgroup, p = 0.256), and the signal is a change concurrent with conversion. (2) Any classification or detection accuracy. (3) Hippocampal volume, which was not measured. (4) A like-for-like test. CBF was tested as a change (interaction), but volume only cross-sectionally at V1. The PD group as a whole had significant prefrontal atrophy from V0 to V1 (p.6), and volume change was not compared between converters and non-converters. (5) A robust effect. The interaction is uncorrected (the ANOVAs use p < 0.05, unlike the FDR-corrected analyses, p.4), it appears in 1 of 14 ROIs, it rests on 10 converters, and the reported partial eta2 = 0.90 looks implausible for F = 4.66. Converters also had much less education (9.3 vs 12.6 years, p = 0.005), which is not listed as a covariate in that ANOVA. (6) The population is Parkinson's, not AD-spectrum. Narrowed form: PARTLY, and weak. A non-volumetric (perfusion) measure tracked conversion where the tested cortical volumes did not, but the comparator is not hippocampal volume, and the effect is marginal and uncorrected. Independence: new dataset and new method family (ASL perfusion). No authors or site shared with supporters. Peer-reviewed (Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience 2022).

quotes.quote: In patients with PD, converters showed a more significant CBF reduction (25.8%) than non-converters at V1(7.8%) in the left lateral orbitofrontal cortex (Figure 2B). A marginal subgroup difference was found in the left lateral orbitofrontal cortex, an interaction between subgroup and visit was found [F(1,96) = 4.66, p = 0.036, partial η2 = 0.90] in addition to an effect of visit [F(1) = 16.0, p < 0.001, partial η2 = 0.254]. No main effect of the subgroup was found (p = 0.256). No effect of the subgroup was found in any other prefrontal ROIs (ps > 0.145).

Converters were similar to non-converters at V1 in the total intracranial volume (p = 0.452), total cortical grey matter volume (p = 0.737), and the volume of prefrontal ROIs (ps > 0.150). However, from V0 to V1, subjects with PD showed a significantly cortical atrophy in the bilateral lateral orbitofrontal cortex (left: t(48) = 2.91, p = 0.005; right: t(48) = 2.98, p = 0.005)
Importantly, longitudinal changes in the prefrontal CBF did not correlate with those in the prefrontal volume (ps > 0.369).

Third, we explored whether converters showed a more significant prefrontal CBF reduction than non-converters using repeated-measures ANOVAs (p < 0.05) with two factors, subgroups (converters and non-converters) and visit (V0 and V1).

Although patients with PD showed additional cortical atrophy in the prefrontal cortex, prefrontal volumetric reduction did not significantly contribute to the progression of MCI or executive dysfunction.
First, the small patient pool subsequently led to fewer patients in the converter subgroup, thus, probably resulting in bias.
